blocks.text: You began as a single fertilised egg. By the time you finished secondary school that one cell had become roughly thirty trillion cells, every one of them carrying the same 46 chromosomes. Only one process can copy a cell that faithfully, that many times — mitosis.

blocks.markdown:
## Two kinds of division, two jobs

**Mitosis** produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent and have the same chromosome number. It is used for growth, for replacing worn-out cells and for asexual reproduction.

**Meiosis** produces four daughter cells, each with **half** the chromosome number of the parent and each genetically different. It occurs only in the reproductive organs and produces gametes.

A cell with the full set of chromosomes in pairs is **diploid** (written $2n$). A cell with only one chromosome from each pair is **haploid** ($n$). In humans $2n = 46$ and $n = 23$.

blocks.title: Homologous chromosomes
blocks.text: A matching pair of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent, carrying genes for the same characteristics in the same order. Meiosis separates the members of every homologous pair; mitosis never does.

blocks.markdown:
### Interphase comes first

Before any division the cell spends most of its life in **interphase**, during which it grows, makes proteins and — critically — copies every chromosome so that each becomes two identical **chromatids** joined at a centromere. Interphase is not a stage of mitosis, but nothing can divide without it.

blocks.title: The stages of mitosis in order
blocks.prompt: Describe what happens to the chromosomes at each stage of mitosis in an animal cell.

steps.text: Prophase — the chromosomes shorten and thicken until they are visible as pairs of chromatids. The nuclear membrane and nucleolus break down and the centrioles move to opposite poles, forming spindle fibres.
Metaphase — the chromosomes line up singly across the middle of the cell (the equator) and each centromere attaches to a spindle fibre.
Anaphase — the centromeres divide and the spindle fibres contract, pulling one chromatid of each pair to each pole. Each chromatid is now a full chromosome.
Telophase — a nuclear membrane re-forms around each group of chromosomes, the chromosomes lengthen and become invisible again, and the nucleolus reappears.
Cytokinesis — the cytoplasm divides. In an animal cell the membrane pinches inwards; in a plant cell a new cell plate forms across the middle and a cellulose wall is laid down.

blocks.answer: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis — giving two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. Remember the order with 'PMAT'.

blocks.markdown:
### Meiosis in outline

Meiosis is two divisions one after the other.

**Meiosis I** is the reduction division. Homologous chromosomes pair up (**synapsis**) to form bivalents, and while paired they may exchange segments — **crossing over**. The pairs then line up at the equator and whole chromosomes, not chromatids, are pulled to opposite poles. Each of the two cells produced is now haploid.

**Meiosis II** resembles mitosis: the chromatids of each chromosome separate. The final result is four haploid cells.

Two events make every gamete genetically unique: crossing over, and the random way each homologous pair lines up (**independent assortment**).

blocks.title: Why halving matters
blocks.text: If gametes were diploid, fertilisation would double the chromosome number in every generation. Meiosis halves it beforehand, so a haploid sperm plus a haploid egg restores exactly the diploid number — 23 + 23 = 46 in humans.

blocks.title: Common WAEC trap
blocks.text: In anaphase of mitosis, chromatids separate. In anaphase I of meiosis, whole chromosomes separate. Getting these two the wrong way round is the single most common error on this topic.

points: Chromosomes are copied during interphase before any division begins.
Mitosis follows the order prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase and gives two identical diploid cells.
Meiosis involves two divisions and gives four genetically different haploid cells.
Crossing over and independent assortment in meiosis are the origin of genetic variation in sexual reproduction.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that fertilisation restores the diploid number rather than doubling it.
